Armed Conflict & Security
• Ukraine launched a coordinated missile and drone strike that partially collapsed sections of the Kerch (Crimea) bridge, a key logistics link for Russia; Moscow vowed to repair the damage amid retaliatory strikes on Ukrainian infrastructure.
• A 72-year-old Palestinian woman was shot dead in the West Bank in an incident involving Israeli settlers; Palestinians say it was an attack, while the Israeli military says settlers returned fire after being attacked.
• Houthi gains toward Aden are galvanizing Yemen’s southern separatists, as Saudi Arabia reshuffles military leadership to counter the advance.
• Reports citing unnamed U.S. officials allege Iran is exploring a “dirty bomb” plot in Washington; President Trump issued a public warning as Tehran denies involvement.
• A Costa Rican journalist covering narco-politics was killed by gunmen, highlighting rising risks to reporters amid regional drug violence.
Why it matters: Escalating strikes in Ukraine, growing West Bank settler violence, and shifting fronts in Yemen all underscore widening regional volatility, while alleged terror plotting and attacks on journalists add to global security concerns and democratic backsliding risks.

Society & Human Rights.title: Hero, villain or victim: why are refugees so rarely seen now as fully human? | Zoe Williams
Society & Human Rights.text:
The understanding of refugees as complex individuals, motivated variously by wanting to build a new life and return to what was theirs, often seems to have been lost. A new film offers a different, truer, perspectiveThere was a screening last week of Seize the Summit, which follows four refugees as they try to reach the top of Kilimanjaro. It was organised by a recent MA graduate from Goldsmiths, with a panel afterwards, which I was set to chair. So she and I were spitballing what the film-maker, Arwa Damon, would want to talk about, and Hanya, the graduate, said: “I think her purpose is to mainstream the idea of the refugee as a human being.” It was such a stark statement that we both started laughing.There are many categories of refugee in current affairs storytelling. There’s the desperate victim; the criminal, or criminal-waiting-to-happen; the hero, battling unimaginable odds, though this tends to be a retrospective narrative, ie second-generation members of a diaspora talking about their parents. There are refugees en masse, shorn of any traits or qualities at all, discussed purely in terms of whether or not the host state can accommodate them, and how long they should be allowed to stay in any given place.Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnistThe Guardian’s year in review 2026

Instead, the latest chapter of its Made of Makers™ program brings video games, often called the "10th Art," into a cross-disciplinary roster that already counts sound artist Zimoun, musician TØKIO M¥ERS, street light-painter Roy Wang and pastry chef Nina Métayer.This time, the Maker in the spotlight is Zain Memon, a Mumbai-born, Goa-based storyteller widely regarded as India's most influential game designer. The self-taught creative is best known for SHASN, a political strategy board game that won the Social Impact Award at IndieCade Europe, and its sequel SHASN: AZADI. He’s now deep into MAYA, a sprawling transmedia universe spanning novels, graphic novels, board games and film. For Le Voyer, the board-game pedigree was the point. Unlike mobile games built on quick dopamine hits, board games ask players to sit with a system for hours, making Memon a more natural fit than any digital agency.The result is The Valley of Inventions, an escape game set inside the Manufacture-Atelier at the Maison's origins, with the player stepping into the role of Élie LeCoultre as he inherits the secrets of the trade. Progress hinges on understanding how watchmaking works: iconic complications and inventions, from the chronograph and minute repeater to the tourbillon, perpetual calendar and worldtime, are reimagined as enigmas, interwoven with puzzles about the Vallée de Joux and the Manufacture's many métiers.The game launches globally today as a free app and web experience in seven languages, before taking on physical form: a city-wide hunt across Dubai in December, an in-store activation for clients, a phygital edition gifted to select collectors and, in 2027, a three-room escape-room exhibition in Hong Kong. Of his visit to the Manufacture, Memon says, "It wasn't a question of what to include in the game; it was a question of what I should keep out."Below, Memon and Le Voyer talk us through the making of The Valley of Inventions.What made video games feel like the right next language for Jaeger-LeCoultre?Matthieu Le Voyer: When we came up with the idea, I remember teasing it last year with some journalists, and people told me, "How do you think you can create a video game fighting against Blizzard and Activision? It's impossible." And I told them, "Look, we're looking at things through a different prism." I'm not going to do the next Call of Duty. That's not what we have in mind.What we are looking for through video games is to reach new audiences, but we need to maintain our own identity and DNA. I don't want to dilute what Jaeger-LeCoultre is, which is all about intellect, culture, art and visual expression. Everyone plays those small games on the metro, like Candy Crush or Clash of Clans. That's probably not what we need either. We need something halfway: on one side you have that, and on the other you have a centuries-old industry that needs new levers to communicate its message. It's about how you create the storytelling and make it feel relevant, not just opportunistic. I didn't want to do something cool for the sake of saying, "Hey, I'm cool.""With board games, you're not playing for the quick adrenaline or dopamine hit of a mobile game. It has to be well thought out, because you need to sit for one or two hours." – Matthieu Le Voyer, CMO, Jaeger-LeCoultre And why Zain, of all the game designers you could have worked with?Matthieu Le Voyer: Because he started with board games. With board games, you're not playing for the quick adrenaline or dopamine hit of a mobile game. It has to be well thought out, because you need to sit for one or two hours and the mechanics have to get players deeply involved. When the team suggested working with someone who develops board games, I thought it was a brilliant idea, because the bridge from board games to this type of video game is much easier than working with an agency that builds addictive mobile games. We curated board game designers and discovered Zain. What struck me was that he's building a multimedia universe bridging physical board games and digital games, in a very humble way a kind of Lord of the Rings environment. That meant he would be able to bridge all the touchpoints and media.Zain, coming from board games, how did you decide what would become the gameplay for this project?Zain Memon: Be it my games, my novels, whatever I've worked on, my objective has always been: how do I take something that's complex and beautiful and make it accessible to more people?I remember very vividly going to the Maison in the Vallée de Joux, checking out the archives and how the watches are made, and realizing that even though I thought I knew so much about watches, the amount of care, love and precision there was the purest form of engineering meets art. It wasn't a question of what to include in the game; it was a question of what I should keep out, because everything, from the history to the patents to the mechanisms, was so exciting. I was like a kid in a candy store. The entire focus was: how do I get someone who doesn't necessarily understand watches to really understand what precision instrument design looks like? I believe that after playing this game, you will get a sense of how deep the world of Jaeger-LeCoultre is.Matthieu Le Voyer: Understanding how a perpetual calendar or a tourbillon works is not easy. Building a complete gear train, from the power reserve to the regulating organ, is even more complicated. The first challenge for us was to transmit this knowledge to Zain so he could digest it and make it playful.Can you hint at what you couldn't fit into the game when it came to capturing the essence of watchmaking?Zain Memon: I met watchmakers and master watchmakers who have been working on one complication for six or eight years, perfecting what it takes to create a minute repeater, for example. More than the engineering precision, it's the amount of love it takes, because one micrometer away and the watch doesn't work anymore. So I think I've managed to capture maybe the top sliver of what it really means to make a watch. What I would really like is for people to understand watchmaking better after playing, and perhaps enter that journey themselves, because that journey, to me, is a lifetime of wonder.The game turns watchmaking complications and inventions into enigmas. How did you approach designing those puzzles?Zain Memon: When I'm structuring a puzzle, it breaks into three parts. The first is intrigue: how does this thing work? The second is: how do I translate it into something that lets people understand watchmaking? And the third movement is the "aha" moment, where the new knowledge clicks and you understand the watch better. Take the minute repeater: how do I take an auditory mechanism that chimes perfectly, tell people what it is, explain how it works and then let them use it? Once you complete that chain, the player feels fulfilled because they've not only learned something, they've also solved a puzzle. We are crisscrossing learning with wonder constantly.Matthieu Le Voyer: Just to give you a hint: how would you transform the chime of a minute repeater into a lock? There are a few like this.Matthieu, video games are often framed as the defining medium of 21st-century pop culture. How do you know when a new medium genuinely extends the Maison's story, rather than simply modernizing it?Matthieu Le Voyer: The challenge is always to do something that respects your DNA. What would be extremely risky would be to create something that's cool but has no relevance to Jaeger-LeCoultre. Whenever we discuss how to expand Made of Makers, it's with the same idea: how can we transmit the story of Jaeger-LeCoultre in a way that gets people interested?To me, it's a gateway to bring new people toward watchmaking. When you're a kid, there is nothing you remember as well as something you learned through play. You even see it with babies learning languages: when it's a game, it's long-lasting. So we're creating a medium that generates curiosity and lasting memories. The message remains the same: Jaeger-LeCoultre, the Manufacture, complications, artistry, the Watchmaker of Watchmakers. We're packaging that message in something that sparks interest among new people. “I think I've managed to capture maybe the top sliver of what it really means to make a watch." – Zain Memon Zain Memon: What really worked for us is that we were translating across different media from the word go. Matthieu's vision was very clear: "We want this to be a digital game, but we also want people to experience it physically and have an intimate, tactile experience with the watches and the Manufacture." Often when you make a video game, you design for a digital UI/UX, and that limits what you can do physically. Here it was the other way around. Even digitally, when you enter the room, it feels like you're part of it: you're picking up objects, placing them, making them click together. Having that vision set out so clearly helped us translate almost exactly what the video game feels like.Matthieu Le Voyer: There were things that were impossible to translate. In digital, you can do whatever you want. With a perpetual calendar, you can manipulate it backwards and forwards. But if you're a watch connoisseur, you know a two-way perpetual calendar is a complication worth hundreds of thousands of euros. You can't build a lock that costs the price of our most expensive watches! So we had to find bypasses and re-engineer locks using existing elements to match what was physically feasible.Matthieu, why bring the escape room to Hong Kong?Matthieu Le Voyer: Today there is a lot of commercial and marketing noise, so when we address a market, we want to make a splash and be visible. The Collectibles exhibition was just the beginning of our Hong Kong strategy, and we're going to do more there in the coming months. We chose Hong Kong for this exhibition because the level of connoisseurship there is among the top of the top worldwide. It's the right place to see the interplay between video games and watch connoisseurs, and if it proves successful, the plan is to roll it out in other markets next year.The Valley of Inventions is now available for free on app and web. The Hong Kong exhibition opens in 2027.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: AAPE Taps LNGSHOT Again for Its FW26 “AAPE UNDERGROUND” Collection

Entertainment.title: 007's New Watch Dilemma: Will Robert Pattinson Bring Jaeger-LeCoultre to MI6?
Entertainment.text: The announcement that Robert Pattinson will officially step into the tuxedo as the next James Bond didn’t just shake up the film industry—it set off a high-stakes turf war in the luxury watch world. For 31 years, Omega has enjoyed an ironclad, incredibly lucrative grip on the 007 franchise. Since GoldenEye in 1995, every cinematic iteration of the British spy has checked his Omega Seamaster before saving the world.But Pattinson’s arrival introduces a massive complication: just months before being unveiled as the new Bond, he was named a global brand ambassador for Jaeger-LeCoultre (JLC).The Commercial Tug-of-WarWhen Pattinson appeared in his official Bond announcement photos, watch enthusiasts immediately noticed the glaring detail: his wrist was bare. This conspicuous absence is fueling rampant speculation about a behind-the-scenes battle between two Swiss giants.Historically, the actor playing Bond naturally absorbs the Omega partnership—both Pierce Brosnan and Daniel Craig became direct Omega ambassadors during their respective tenures. But Pattinson enters the franchise with an active, high-profile contract with a rival, Richemont-owned brand.While Jaeger-LeCoultre will undoubtedly push hard to break Omega’s three-decade exclusivity streak and finally put a JLC on 007's wrist, Omega (backed by the massive marketing budget of the Swatch Group) is unlikely to surrender its most iconic cultural pillar without a fierce financial fight. The ultimate compromise might see Pattinson retaining his JLC ties off-screen while dutifully wearing Omega on-camera—but if the franchise decides to pivot, JLC has the perfect arsenal for a modern Bond.What Could a JLC Bond Wear?If 007 makes the unprecedented switch, here are the Jaeger-LeCoultre pieces that would perfectly fit the life of a cinematic super-spy:Jaeger-LeCoultre Polaris DateIf Bond needs a direct substitute for his trusty Omega Seamaster, the Polaris Date is the obvious choice. Inspired by JLC's iconic 1968 diver, it features 200 meters of water resistance, an inner rotating bezel (adjusted via the secondary crown), and a rugged rubber strap. It is tough enough for an underwater infiltration sequence, yet refined enough to peek out from under the cuff of a tactical wet suit.Jaeger-LeCoultre Reverso TributeBond is just as famous for his high-stakes casino scenes as he is for his action sequences, and the Reverso is the ultimate tuxedo watch. Originally designed in 1931 for polo players, the case flips over to protect the dial from physical impact. In the hands of MI6’s Q Branch, however, that blank steel caseback is begging to be modified into a hidden communication screen, a laser cutter, or a biometric tracker.Jaeger-LeCoultre Polaris Mariner MemovoxA step up in complexity from the standard Polaris, the Mariner Memovox is a serious ISO 6425-compliant dive watch boasting 300 meters of water resistance. What makes it perfect for Bond is its signature "Memovox" mechanical alarm complication, which rings via a striking mechanism inside the case. It’s a beautifully analogue tool for a spy who needs a precise countdown timer for a ticking bomb or a synchronized extraction.Jaeger-LeCoultre Master Control Chronograph CalendarFor a globe-trotting agent who needs a watch that bridges the gap between field work and the boardroom, the Master Control Chronograph Calendar hits the sweet spot. It offers the sporty utility of a stopwatch—ideal for timing high-speed pursuits or precise tactical movements—wrapped in a highly elegant, mid-century-inspired case that pairs flawlessly with a suit.Jaeger-LeCoultre Master Ultra Thin MoonWhen the mission requires Bond to blend into the ultra-wealthy elite at a billionaire's gala, he needs a watch of pure, understated sophistication. The Master Ultra Thin Moon is impossibly sleek and elegant, slipping effortlessly under a dress shirt. Its stealthy profile makes it the ultimate "quiet luxury" piece, allowing 007 to look impeccably sharp without drawing unwanted attention to his wrist.Whether the producers stick with the tried-and-true Seamaster or allow Pattinson's JLC loyalties to infiltrate MI6, the battle for Bond's wrist is suddenly the most interesting subplot in Hollywood.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: Slam Jam and Levi’s Reunite for a Star-Studded Custom Denim Collection
Entertainment.text: SummarySlam Jam and Levi's have joined forces for the third chapter of their ongoing collaborative partnershipThe DIY-inspired project reimagines deadstock denim with black-painted seams and custom star-shaped metal studsThe collection officially drops on November 19 at Slam Jam locations, SKP-S Beijing, and Worksout SeoulSlam Jam and Levi's have joined forces once more, officially introducing the third chapter of their ongoing partnership with a custom take on the 501 Original and Trucker Jacket. Rooted in the DIY practices that have long shaped denim culture, the latest collaborative project breathes new life into deadstock garments, celebrating customization as an instinctive form of self-expression.Approaching the Levi’s archive with a rebellious attitude, Slam Jam injects its distinct visual vocabulary into the classic silhouettes. The collection is highlighted by the Italian institution's upside-down "A" logo, which has been reimagined as a star-shaped metal stud. These custom hardware additions run across both the Trucker Jacket and the 501 Original jeans, serving as wishful badges that embody the community's restlessness and urge for change.Adding further contrast to the raw aesthetic, both pieces feature striking black-painted external seams. Drawing from a deep pool of cultural references—spanning from military insignia and punk counterculture to David Bowie's imagery and sports iconography—the star motif solidifies the collection's punk-inspired, DIY ethos.The Slam Jam x Levi’s custom collection drops on November 19 across all Slam Jam retail doors, as well as at SKP-S Beijing and Worksout Seoul. Science & Technology.text: SummaryREO unveils the Runabout truck and SUV lineup.Its utilitarian design prioritizes physical controls, simplicity, and easy repairs.Texas-built models start at $21,500 USD, with deliveries expected by late 2028.The historic American marque REO is officially back, teaming up with Frank Stephenson's eponymous design studio to debut the all-new Runabout range. Powered by petrol, the range consists of the T4X work truck, the T4C crew cab and the S4C family SUV. The lineup is a significant departure away from the bloated, tech-heavy trucks currently dominating the market. Instead, REO is doubling down on a radically simple, right-to-repair ethos, delivering a trio of vehicles engineered to be affordable, easily maintained, and last decades.Visually, the Runabout range grounds itself in its utilitarian aesthetic while still carving out a distinct identity. The upright front grille draws direct inspiration from America’s oldest pick-up, the 1915 REO Speed Wagon, while its broad shoulders and forward-leaning stance are modeled after the American bison. Simplicity and repairability are at the heart of the design. Frankstephenson design opted for standard-size, stacked LED headlights and bolt-on wheel arch extensions that owners can easily source and replace off the shelf if damaged. Inside the cabin, physical controls have been intentionally retained and sized for everyday use, even with thick work gloves on.All three models sit on a shared ladder-frame chassis, utilizing the same wheelbase and front bodywork before diverging into different purpose-built forms. The two-seat T4X features a steel flatbed with drop sides for versatility loading from either the sides or the rear, while the T4C crew cab accommodates five passengers alongside a separate load bed. Rounding out the lineup, the six-seat S4C SUV features the shortest rear overhang of the group and a side-hinged tailgate complete with a fully drop-down window. Committed to their anti-obsolescence ethos, REO plans to make its factory service manual completely free, as well as provide a comprehensive parts catalogue for its owners.Production for the REO Trucks Runabout range will take place at a new facility in Texas. The vehicles are priced for true accessibility, with the T4X starting at just $21,500 USD, the T4C at $25,000 USD, and the S4C at $28,500 USD. Pilot builds for the T4X are slated for 2027, with the first customer deliveries targeted for late 2028 to early 2029. Artificial Intelligence.title: AI Is Giving Optical Computing Another Shot
Artificial Intelligence.text: The idea of computing with light has been around for over 70 years, but until recently it’s remained largely in the realm of research. Over the past few years, though, optical computing has emerged as a fast-growing industry: Market valuation of companies in this sector now totals US $2.22 billion, up from $0.4 billion in 2022. One projection suggests that the market will continue to grow exponentially in the coming years.The reason for this sudden surge will surprise no one: AI. In particular, AI inference—the process of using AI models to respond to user queries—has driven much of the construction of huge, power-hungry data centers, and relatively energy-efficient optical systems are seen as a potential way forward.“Most of the interest in [photonics] is driven by the fact that AI inference has literally become limited by power, and in a rather striking manner,” says Peter McMahon, associate professor of applied and engineering physics at Cornell University, in Ithaca, N.Y., who has researched optical computing for over a decade.Optics, at least on paper, carries the promise of doing the same math as today’s GPUs at a drastically lower level of power. Switching from electronics to optics would be a pretty radical solution. Nevertheless, like mushrooms after a rainstorm, optical-computing startups are popping up in the United States, China, Germany, and Israel. And while competing against such GPU makers as Nvidia is an ambitious goal, the investment in optical computing has spurred development of complementary approaches, such as designing alternative AI algorithms, taking on scientific computing, and enhancing in-network computing. Optalysys, based in England, is inserting optical-computing elements into the networking path, where data centers already use light. The company’s basic on-chip optical element, shown in the inset, is a Fourier transform calculator.Optalysys“I think it would be good for the technology if many of these companies made a good run at it,” says Logan Wright, assistant professor of applied physics at Yale University, in New Haven, Conn., and a former postdoc in McMahon’s lab. “I think that the technology that will be developed through this would be really, really useful, and enable photonic systems that maybe don’t get on this wave of AI but would be capable of doing really quite special things.”Optics to inference’s rescue? Inference makes up the bulk of AI energy use. The industry is already spending billions of dollars designing advanced GPUs and other chips to run inference as efficiently as possible. At the heart of the inference computation is one operation, done countless times a second: matrix-vector multiplication.Back in 1978, optical-computing pioneer Joseph W. Goodman and his coworkers proposed a method for doing matrix-vector multiplication with light. The setup was relatively simple. Let’s say a vector of length N needs to be multiplied by a matrix of size N by N. N light-emitting diodes, all in a row, encode the elements of the vector into the intensity of light—the brighter the light from an individual diode, the greater the value that diode encodes. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads out the light vertically, essentially copying the vector N times. The light then passes through an attenuator of N by N pixels. At each pixel, the light is attenuated according to the corresponding value at that location in the matrix. Passing the light through the attenuator performs the multiplication. Finally, a cylindrical lens oriented perpendicular to the first lens re-collects the light from each row, summing it up. The final vector is measured by a row of detectors.VECTOR-MATRIX MULTIPLICATIONThe most computationally expensive part of common AI today is vector-matrix (or matrix-matrix) multiplication. For a vector of length N (here, N = 3), it takes N2 (here, 9) multiplication steps and three accumulation steps—multiple additions at once. The argument for why optics might be advantageous over electronics goes something like this: Multiplying a matrix of size N by N by a vector of length N takes N2 multiplication steps. In electronics, each multiplication takes some energy, so the total energy used scales as N2. In optics, however, the multiplication step is passive: As long as the matrix stays the same, passing light through the attenuator costs almost no energy. The only cost is encoding the vector into light and reading out the answer, but the vector is of length N, not N2. So the energy used will scale as N, not N2, as bigger vectors and matrices are multiplied.Since Goodman’s 1978 proposal, the quality of the available optical elements has improved dramatically. Indeed, in 2022, a team of researchers at Cornell led by McMahon demonstrated an optical neural network that consumed less than one photon of energy—approximately 2.5 x 10-19 joules—per multiplication operation. In a standard computer, a single multiply operation can take between 10-14 and 10-12 joules, which suggests that optics could possibly reduce energy use by a factor of 100,000.But McMahon cautions against such extrapolation. First, the cost of encoding data into optics was not included in the calculation. Even if the scaling is favorable with light, in practice it’s not just the scaling that matters, it’s also the coefficients. Let’s say the energy cost of doing one multiplication with electronics is 1 picojoule, and the cost to encode one vector element with optics is 1,000 picojoules. The electronic approach still wins if the length N of the vector is fewer than 1,000 elements.McMahon says this example is not far off from reality: “One of the key questions is, How big do you have to make the system before you start winning? Lots of people have done this calculation for various kinds of neural networks. The very rough answer is somewhere between N equals 1,000 and N equals 10,000.”It’s also important to keep in mind a computing principle known as Amdahl’s law.“Amdahl’s law shouldn’t even be called a law. It’s a simple piece of common sense,” McMahon says. “If you have something that’s going to accelerate a computation, and it can accelerate 90 percent of the code, but there’s 10 percent of the code that it can’t accelerate, then the maximum possible speedup you can get is 10x.”With AI inferencing, the point is to save energy, not time. But Amdahl’s observation still applies. What fraction of today’s AI inferencing code can be better handled with optics is a complicated question that varies by approach. But it’s not 100 percent. Matrix-vector multiplication, or matrix-matrix multiplication, is only part of the inference workload—there are other, nonlinear operations that need to be performed on the data.Taking all of these caveats into account, optical-computing companies today are aiming for a 10- to 80-fold improvement in energy efficiency over today’s GPUs. The question is whether they can deliver on that promise at scale before traditional electronics catches up to those gains.Bridging the gap in free spaceThe startup Lumai, based in Oxford, England, has taken perhaps the most direct inspiration from Goodman and his team. Lumai’s head of product, Phillip Burr, declares that a free-space approach, where the light travels through air rather than on-chip waveguides, is what will enable the company’s tech to beat GPUs.Instead of the fixed attenuator used in Goodman’s proposal, Lumai is using a modern programmable device called a spatial light modulator—a pixelated membrane akin to a fancy liquid-crystal display that can modulate both the intensity and phase of light. The rest of the design is more sophisticated in practice but similar in principle to Goodman’s design: A vector is encoded into light, copied N times via a lens, passed through the spatial light modulator, collected with another lens, and the result is converted back to digital electronics. The electronics then handle the nonlinear functions. “A full vector-matrix multiply completes in a single optical cycle,” Burr says.To accurately compare the energy expenditures of the optical and GPU approaches, you must first specify which part of the workload you’re considering. Modern inference is often split into two phases: prefill, where the input query is processed and propagated through the model, and decode, where the output is generated one word (or token) at a time. Prefill is the more computationally intensive of the two. It basically involves doing vector-matrix multiplications for the same matrix over and over. Decode also involves vector-matrix multiplies, but not as intensively—the time-consuming part of decode is reading the necessary matrices in and out of memory.Vector-matrix multiplication with free-space opticsThe Goodman optical computer is the simplest version of a photonic vector-matrix multiplier. Here, the vector elements are encoded into the intensity of light from three light sources, such as LEDs. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads the light vertically. The matrix elements are encoded into the opacity of an attenuator, such that when light passes through each pixel it is multiplied (attenuated) by that matrix value. Finally, another cylindrical lens collects the light horizontally, performing the accumulation step, and a photodetector measures the output vector. Lumai, and other companies in the space, are focusing on the compute-intensive prefill phase of inference. Lumai claims that its Iris Nova optical server, made available for evaluation in April 2026, is a proof of concept, and its next-generation Iris Aura server will do prefill using roughly one-tenth of the energy a GPU would use.The startup Neurophos, based in Austin, Texas, is putting a different spin on the Goodman computer design. To pack more punch into a small device, the company is leveraging its expertise in metamaterials—complex structures that can manipulate light at scales smaller than a single wavelength. The structures it has designed are bigger than a wavelength but still quite small—just several micrometers per side.“The equivalent of the optical transistor that you can get from standard silicon photonics today is like 2 millimeters long,” says Patrick Bowen, CEO of Neurophos. “You just can’t fit enough [of] them on-chip to get a compute density that remotely competes with the latest and greatest [that] TSMC [Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.] does.”Bowen’s team designed metamaterial-based modulators that can be programmed to manipulate the phase and intensity of light at the micrometer scale, resulting in an array of 1,000 by 1,000 modulators in a square chip with 5-mm sides. According to Bowen, Neurophos’s modulators switch over 10,000 times as fast as a standard liquid-crystal spatial light modulators do.Bowen also claims a performance advantage over Nvidia’s Blackwell GPU: “We’re targeting 50 times Blackwell B200’s speed and 35 times its energy efficiency, and have a road map to reach 250 times the speed and roughly 90 times the energy efficiency in subsequent generations.”The approach is CMOS-compatible, Bowen says, which should allow Neurophos to manufacture its chips on the semiconductor industry’s existing high-volume production lines. The company is currently choosing a site for a production facility ahead of its rack deliveries to customers in 2028.Both Lumai and Neurophos are betting they’ll get their products to market before traditional CMOS can catch up to their energy savings. “Silicon will keep improving, but digital efficiency gains now come slowly and at rising cost,” Burr says. “Optics offers a different scaling relationship, in which efficiency improves as matrices grow. Larger models, longer context windows, and agentic workloads are all pushing prefill in that direction.”Bridging the gap on-chipFree-space optics carries the promise of almost energy-free multiplication, as in Goodman’s design. But another big advance in optics since Goodman’s work in the 1970s is integrated photonics, which allows you to guide and manipulate light on-chip.“The name of the game is to do as large a vector size as possible to maximize the benefit of using optics, and for that reason the free-space approaches are promising,” says Yale’s Logan Wright. “But it’s still fundamentally harder” to use the free-space approach, “because there’s just so much less infrastructure than in silicon photonics.”Other companies—like Shanghai-based Lightelligence and Q.ANT, based in Stuttgart, Germany—are trading the 3D advantage of free-space optics for the manufacturability of photonics integrated directly onto a silicon chip.“There is a good reason that free-space optics are usually limited to 1,000 units a year,” says Q.ANT’s CEO and founder, Michael Förtsch. “The reason for this is lens inspection, assembly strategy, and so on. Semiconductor-manufacturable integrated photonic circuits are at this point way more promising to reach volume production.”Vector-matrix multiplication with integrated photonicsOne way to do vector-matrix multiplication with light on-chip involves encoding vector elements into the amplitudes of pulses of light, traveling sequentially through a waveguide. The multiplication is performed by Mach-Zehnder interferometers: A waveguide splits in two, and the phase of light traveling through one of the paths is shifted by a controlled voltage. When the two paths reunite, the resulting light intensity depends on that phase shift, performing a multiplication. Encoding the matrix elements into the phase shifts turns this into vector-matrix multiplication. A photodetector then collects the light from all three pulses, performing the accumulation step.In Q.ANT’s approach, the input data is encoded into the phase and amplitude of light pulses via on-chip modulators. A vector in this scheme is represented as a sequence of such pulses, each representing one vector element. The light is guided around the chip with waveguides. The basic computational element is an interferometer: A waveguide splits into two paths, and the light beam traveling down one path is subjected to a phase shift, controlled by a set voltage. When the two paths recombine, the resulting interference performs a computation. Then, photodetectors and analog-to-digital converters turn the result back into digital data. The serialized vector-matrix multiplication approach is slower than Goodman’s computer, where the whole calculation happens at once. However, the slower speed can be mitigated by using multiple wavelengths at once, effectively encoding multiple vectors into light simultaneously.Q.ANT’s Native Processing Server is already being used in research institutions like the Leibniz Supercomputing Centre in Munich and the Jülich Supercomputing Centre in Jülich, both in Germany. Earlier this year, the company announced a commercial sale to the cloud provider Ionos. Similarly, Lightelligence’s PACE2 processor is capable of multiplying 128-by-128-element matrices. In a paper released in 2025, the company described vector-matrix multiplication at a 1-gigahertz frequency and 3-nanosecond latency, claiming two orders of magnitude lower latency than with traditional GPUs.The energy advantage is yet to be conclusively demonstrated, however, and Q.ANT’s Förtsch admits there is still a ways to go. The main issue is the energy cost of analog-to-digital conversion and back. As long as a fast, low-energy converter does not exist, Förtsch says, “we don’t see realistic chances that…a general vector-matrix multiplication machine in optics makes sense.”Beyond matrix-vector multiplicationNot everyone in the field is focused on matrix-vector multiplication, despite it being all the rage in the AI inference world. In fact, while the optical vector-matrix multiply idea goes back to the 1970s, other computations with optics have been investigated as far back as the 1950s. For example, a Fourier transform—a common operation that decomposes a complex wave or signal into its constituent frequencies—can be done in optics with a single lens.“A digital chip has to approximate [Fourier transforms] in many small steps, using hundreds to thousands of transistors and more compute cycles,” says Q.ANT’s Förtsch. “Models that use such nonlinear functions can reach the same or better accuracy with fewer parameters and fewer operations.”Even though Q.ANT’s optical processor has been used for traditional vector-matrix multiplication, the company believes its greatest advantages lie in alternative AI architectures that leverage more complex functions. “Tasks such as image classification and segmentation rely heavily on operations like Fourier series, transformations, and other nonlinear functions, which photonics handles natively. We see similar potential in generative AI, especially image and video generation,” Förtsch says.The Israel-based startup LightSolver is also targeting algorithms that are a more natural fit for its device. “If you look at propagating electromagnetic waves, essentially, they are running differential equations in their nature,” says Ruti Ben-Shlomi, CEO and cofounder of LightSolver. She says differential equations can be solved much faster and with higher energy efficiency on the company’s laser processing unit (LPU) than on a traditional computer.LightSolver’s LPU is an interesting twist on the Goodman optical-computer design. It has input light, a programmable membrane in the form of a spatial light modulator, and output light, but the whole thing is placed in a cavity, where light bounces back and forth many times before reaching a steady state. In addition, the team places a gain medium inside the cavity. This gain medium functions much like those found inside a laser, causing the bouncing light to build up in intensity.  LightSolver, a startup based in Israel, is using free-space optics to quickly solve differential equations by harnessing the natural properties of light. LightSolverOnce a particular problem is encoded into the modulator, the gain medium is stimulated to emit random photons. They bounce back and forth, increasing in intensity when passing through the gain medium again, experiencing preprogrammed changes through the modulator and interacting with one another until they reach a steady state—the solution. Then, a simple camera takes a picture of the steady-state result. Using emulation, the LightSolver team recently showed that their LPU can solve differential equations 40 to 80,000 times as fast as a GPU, depending on the workflow. They are now working on explicitly benchmarking the energy improvements.LightSolver’s team is currently working on AI applications for its LPU as well, using the company’s own algorithm to do image generation from text. “We’re not doing vector-matrix multiplication very fast. We are doing something different. We need to assume that the way you train the model, and you then do inference, is completely different. But if you do it differently, you’ll be able to do image generation with dramatic energy-consumption decrease and speedup,” Ben-Shlomi says. LightSolver has a working prototype of its LPU, and the team is working on a larger, rack-mountable box.Computing in transitYet another way to leverage light’s particular strengths is being pursued by Optalysys, a startup based in Leeds, England. Nick New, founder and chief product officer, has a background in free-space optics, and so he understood that taking a Fourier transform is very easy to do with light.The key idea behind Optalysys’s technology is taking that Fourier capability of optics in free space and making it work on-chip. “Rather than using a lens these days, we have our own component, which is a passive component in the plane of the silicon that does that same job,” New says. And by cleverly designing that component with multiple outputs, the team figured out how to perform different operations as well. “Because of how the Fourier transform response is generated, you can actually pull out different mathematical operations from it,” New says. “We can produce very large, high-precision digital functions at superhigh efficiencies, using our analog photonics approach.”“We’re effectively adding processing to where there is none right now.” —Nick New, OptalysisInstead of redesigning an accelerator from scratch, Optalysys is targeting a piece of the AI workload that’s often already in the optical domain: networking. In the data center, racks of computers are connected to each other with fiber optics, and the optical connections are increasingly getting closer and closer to the GPUs and CPUs themselves.Some computations already happen while the data is en route. These computations, which include combining results from multiple GPUs, are executed inside network switch cards. But the cards naturally use power to do that math. With passive optical components, these computations could be done essentially for free.New says that in addition to communication between GPUs, Optalysys’s technology could be used to facilitate a GPU’s communication with memory, doing things like compression and format conversion on the fly. Going back to AI inference, this approach could improve the decode part of the workload. Unlike prefill, decode is memory bound: The most costly part is shuffling model data in and out of memory. “We’re more focused on the memory-bound applications, which fits very well with this principle of adding processing into the communication path,” New says. “We’re effectively adding processing to where there is none right now.”The likely future of optical computingHow likely are optical computers to replace GPUs in the data center? Yale’s Wright is not too optimistic. “The direction of algorithm development is not going to be a direction that is automatically favorable for optics,” he says. “In fact, it’s most likely to go in the opposite direction, because [AI model developers] want it to work better on GPUs.”However, even if our AI queries aren’t going to be computed in light in the next few years, that investment in the technology won’t be in vain. Says Wright, “The reason that I and many other people in the field are at least somewhat optimistic is that there’s real investment from companies like Nvidia and TSMC in developing co-packaged silicon photonics—not for computing, but for circuit switching and interconnects, and that just kind of opens the door to do a little bit more in the future.”Whether that technology ends up crunching vector-matrix multiplication, doing bespoke simulations, or performing in-network computations, the computing ecosystem seems ripe for a variety of approaches. “We see the data center of the future as heterogeneous: CPUs, GPUs and photonic NPUs [neural processing units] each take on the tasks they are best suited for,” says Q.ANT’s Förtsch. “Running each task on the most efficient hardware can significantly reduce energy use and operating costs.”

Art & Culture.title: Soho House Puts 11,000 Artworks Between Cloth Covers in ‘Soho Art House’
Art & Culture.text: Summary'Soho Art House' is the first book dedicated to the art collection that hangs across roughly 50 Soho House locations in 19 countriesChief Art Director Kate Bryan wrote and edited the cloth-bound volume, which combines essays, conversations and photographyTwelve cultural figures, including Klaus Biesenbach and Helen Fielding, each pick a favorite work from their local HouseSoho House has released Soho Art House, a cloth-bound book that opens up its global art collection, which spans more than 11,000 works, for the first time. Kate Bryan, the club’s Chief Art Director, wrote and edited the volume after spending the past decade curating and caring for the collection, and she organized it as a guided tour through the Houses rather than a straight catalog.The book is built in clear layers. Andrew Carnie writes the foreword, and Bryan’s own writing appears alongside essays from Ferren Gipson, Jennifer Higgie, Suzanne Hudson and Alastair Sooke. Photography of the works in place throughout the clubs runs between the texts, showing how the art lives in bars, bedrooms and hallways instead of on gallery walls.The most personal section hands the selection over to outsiders. Twelve cultural figures each choose a favorite piece from their local House and explain why it matters to them. Neue Nationalgalerie director Klaus Biesenbach takes on Damien Hirst, and novelist Helen Fielding writes about Harland Miller. The book also includes a roundtable moderated by Bryan with Soho House founder Nick Jones, Jonathan Yeo, who first came up with the collection, and writer and curator Francesca Gavin, one of its early collaborators.The collection’s approach explains its size. It follows the model of La Colombe d’Or, the French hotel where artists once traded their work for meals and rooms, inviting artists to contribute pieces and join a worldwide network. Each House leans toward artists who were born, based or trained in its region. Little House Balham shows work by artists from south of the Thames, and Soho House Bangkok features 33 artists born in or based in Thailand.Across its pages, the book covers a wide range of names, including Tracey Emin, Rashid Johnson, Catherine Opie, Bharti Kher, David Shrigley, Tschabalala Self, Ming Smith, Guerrilla Girls and Olafur Eliasson. The Houses featured stretch from Soho House West Hollywood and Soho House New York to Berlin, Mexico City, Stockholm, Mumbai and Barcelona Pool House.Soho Art House is available now via Soho Home in the UK and US.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast
